title: Owen and the Zapping Balloon
markdown:
The air buzzed with excitement for the village fair, but for Owen it buzzed like a thousand nervous bees. The thought of all the noise made his tummy do flip-flops.

Meanwhile Lyra the moth, her wings dusted with moonlight, was captivated by a shiny cherry-red balloon. She fluttered closer, her wings brushing the balloon’s surface. Zzzt. A startling tingle, sharp as a pinprick, shot through her. An invisible pull and a prickle of sparks made her dart away with a surprised squeak.

“She felt it! She felt the zap!” Pippin shrieked.

Dr. Hale, a scientist with twinkling eyes, chuckled. “That’s quite a reaction, Lyra. You felt a little static electricity.”

Owen looked up, his anxiety easing. “Static?”

“Indeed. When the balloon and Lyra’s wings touched, charge moved. Tiny amounts of it, too small to see. Sometimes enough jumps at once, and you feel a zap.” She rubbed the balloon on her woolen scarf and held it near Lyra. Lyra felt the odd pull again, her wings lifting, drawn to the balloon. It was a silent fascinating dance — attraction because of charge, not because the balloon had become a magnet.

Owen’s eyes lit up. He saw it. Not a scary bang, but a predictable dance of tiny forces. He grabbed a dry straw, rubbed it on his sleeve, and brought it near Lyra. The straw attracted her delicate wing scales too.

“Charged things can pull, like a magnet pulls iron — but this is electricity sitting still on the surface, then jumping.” Confidence surged through him.

The next day at the fair, Owen’s booth held a quiet fascination. Beside his model trebuchet was a display: a red balloon, a woolen scarf, a plastic ruler, and a calm Lyra. Owen, his dread replaced by competence, began to explain.

“When I rub this balloon, it picks up charge. Watch Lyra.” As the balloon floated near, her wings lifted. “She’s attracted to the charge. And sometimes, when enough builds up, it can jump with a little zap. That’s static electricity. It’s also what can make your hair stand on end — like charges pushing each other away.”

Children gasped and giggled. Lyra fluttered contentedly. Owen, who had dreaded surprises, had turned a potential prank into wonder. Understanding the zap made it less frightening and more fun. Pippin, who had shrieked, stayed to rub the scarf himself. The fair went on being loud. Owen’s corner, at least, was a known quantity: wool, rubber, a moth, and a spark you could earn on purpose.
characters: Owen (patient builder), Lyra (moth), Dr. Hale (scientist), Pippin (friend)
